locations.name: Xi'an
locations.associated_context: East Syriac Christian and Aramaic inscriptional evidence
locations.description: Xi'an is included as a location because the archaeology catalogue records the Xi'an Stele from this findspot. The related evidence record provides the historical and religious context of the Tang-dynasty inscription.

evidence.title: Tel Dan Stele
evidence.description: The Tel Dan Stele is preserved in three fragments of an Aramaic royal monument discovered in a secondary architectural context at Tel Dan. Its text is commonly associated with an Aramean ruler, often identified as Hazael of Damascus, and refers to the kings of Israel and the House of David; those historical identifications remain matters of epigraphic interpretation.
evidence.significance: Earliest known reference to the House of David outside the Bible.

evidence.title: Zakkur Stele
evidence.description: The Zakkur Stele is a royal Aramaic inscription associated with Zakkur, a ruler of Hamath and Lu'ash. It records a conflict in which Zakkur faced a coalition led by Bar-Hadad of Aram-Damascus and preserves the political language of an early eighth-century royal monument.
evidence.significance: Important source for Aramean political history and the Aramaic language.

evidence.title: Sefire Stele I
evidence.museum: Damascus National Museum / National Museum of Beirut
evidence.description: Sefire Stele I is one of the three basalt treaty stelae from Sefire. The treaty records obligations, guarantees, sanctions, and divine witnesses in the early first millennium BC.
evidence.significance: Longest known Old Aramaic inscription. Key source for Aramaic treaty language and diplomacy.

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Sculptures
evidence.description: The Tell Halaf sculpture group includes monumental stone lions, sphinxes, caryatid figures, and relief orthostats associated with the palace complex of Kapara at Guzana. The carved programme combines local northern Syrian traditions with wider Syro-Hittite and Mesopotamian visual forms, while the exact meaning of individual figures must be interpreted within the palace and city context.
evidence.significance: Major example of Aramean monumental art blending Syro-Hittite and Mesopotamian styles.

evidence.title: Hadad-yith'i Bilingual Statue and Inscription (Tell Fekheriye)
evidence.description: The Hadad-yis'i statue is a monumental figure bearing parallel Akkadian and Aramaic inscriptions. It records the dedication of the statue to the storm god Hadad by Hadad-yis'i, an official associated with Guzana, and provides evidence for the use of two written languages within the same political and religious setting.
evidence.significance: One of the earliest known Aramaic inscriptions and key evidence for early Aramaic script development.

evidence.title: Kilamuwa Stele
evidence.description: The Kilamuwa Stele is a royal monument from Sam'al depicting King Kilamuwa in formal dress beside a written text. Its Phoenician inscription presents the ruler's achievements and relationships with subjects and neighboring powers, illustrating the multilingual and politically connected character of the kingdom.
evidence.significance: Documents the political history of Bit-Gabbar and its relations with Assyria.

evidence.title: Panamuwa I Inscription (Hadad Statue)
evidence.description: The Panamuwa I inscription is carved on a statue of the storm god Hadad from Sam'al and is written in the local Samalian variety of Aramaic. It links the monument to King Panamuwa I and records a royal dedication in which political authority, divine patronage, and the local written tradition are presented together.
evidence.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and Aramean religious practices.

evidence.title: Panamuwa II Inscription
evidence.description: The Panamuwa II inscription is a funerary and commemorative text erected by Bar-Rakib for his father. Written in Samalian Aramaic, it refers to Panamuwa II's death during the campaign of Tiglath-Pileser III and preserves both family memory and the political setting of Sam'al's submission to Assyria.
evidence.significance: Key source for the Samalian dialect and the political history of Bit-Gabbar.
evidence.image_caption: Panamuwa II torso inscription (KAI 215), reproduced from the 1893 Sendschirli excavation publication.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Felix von Luschan et al. (public domain)

evidence.title: Bar Rakib I
evidence.museum: Museum of the Ancient Orient, Istanbul
evidence.description: Bar-Rakib I is the twenty-line building inscription associated with the construction of the second palace at Sam’al between 732 and 727 BC. A verified line-by-line edition is not yet included, so no transcription is fabricated here.
evidence.significance: Among the earliest records using Imperial Aramaic, showing the spread of standardized Aramaic.
evidence.inscription_note: KAI 216 is reported as a twenty-line building inscription. The twenty line slots are preserved here, but the original script and transliteration still require verification against the primary edition. English translations are intentionally blank.

evidence.title: Katumuwa Stele
evidence.description: The Katumuwa Stele is a carved funerary monument for a royal official at Sam'al. Its Aramaic text describes commemorative rites and places the official's memorial presence in the stele, while the accompanying image and wording provide evidence for one mortuary practice rather than a complete account of local beliefs about death or the soul.
evidence.significance: Unique evidence for Aramean beliefs about the afterlife and soul.

evidence.title: Kilamuwa Scepter
evidence.description: The Kilamuwa Scepter is a small gold object, probably a sheath or fitting associated with a ceremonial staff. Its short inscription is conventionally connected with King Kilamuwa and is variously classified as Phoenician or Aramaic, so the object is best treated as evidence for royal display and cross-regional writing practices without forcing a single linguistic label.
evidence.significance: Royal artifact demonstrating the material culture of Aramean kingship and the use of writing in royal dedication.
evidence.image_caption: Kilamuwa scepter or gold sheath in the Pergamon Museum.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Pergamon Museum

evidence.title: Hazael Booty Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Hazael booty inscriptions are short texts on ivory objects bearing the name Hazael, the ruler of Aram-Damascus. The objects are recorded in the Arslan Tash corpus, an Assyrian-period context, but their exact route to the site and whether they represent booty, tribute, or another transfer should not be assumed from the inscription alone.
evidence.significance: Evidence of the wealth and reach of Aram-Damascus under Hazael.

evidence.title: Hazael Horse Frontlet
evidence.description: The Hazael Horse Frontlet is a bronze ceremonial fitting for a horse, inscribed with the name Hazael of Aram-Damascus. Its discovery at the Heraion on Samos records the presence of an object connected with a Levantine ruler in an Aegean sanctuary, but the inscription alone cannot determine whether the frontlet arrived through diplomacy, exchange, dedication, or later movement.
evidence.inscription_note: The artifact carries one continuous Phoenician inscription of 36 characters, read from right to left after rotation. The relief divides it visually into sequences of 25 and 11 characters, but the inscription has no word separators; the script and transliteration below are a normalized reconstruction from the published reading and should be treated cautiously.

inscription_lines.transliteration: znh ntn hdd mn ʿnq lmrʾn hzl bšnt ʿbr mrʾn nhr
inscription_lines.english_translation: [This is] what Hadad has given from Unqi to our lord Hazael in the year when our lord had crossed the river.

evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean diplomatic or trade connections reaching the Aegean world.

evidence.title: Melqart Stele
evidence.description: The Melqart Stele is a basalt royal monument attributed to Bar-Hadad of Aram and dedicated to the god Melqart. Its Aramaic inscription links royal commemoration with divine patronage, while the stele's findspot and the precise historical setting of the dedication remain important parts of its interpretation.
evidence.significance: Important evidence for Aramean royal dedications and religious practices.

evidence.title: Arslan Tash Amulets
evidence.description: The Arslan Tash amulets are small limestone objects carrying incantation texts that invoke protection against harmful beings. They are traditionally associated with the Arslan Tash find context, but their authenticity and archaeological history have been debated; any reconstruction of Aramaic magical practice must therefore distinguish the texts themselves from claims about their provenance.
evidence.significance: If authentic, rare evidence of Aramaic magical and religious practices.

evidence.title: Arslan Tash Ivory Inscription
evidence.description: The Arslan Tash Ivory Inscription is a short text carved on an ivory object from the ancient settlement of Hadatu. Its material and find context place it within the luxury-art and administrative networks of the Euphrates region, although the inscription should not by itself be used to assign every object at the site to Bit-Adini or to one political period.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean artistic production and luxury goods.

evidence.title: Til Barsip Wall Paintings
evidence.description: The Til Barsip wall paintings are polychrome decorations from the palace complex at Tell Ahmar, ancient Til Barsip. Their scenes include courtly and military imagery and belong to the Assyrian-period transformation of a former Bit-Adini center, so they preserve both local architectural context and imperial visual conventions.
evidence.significance: Rare surviving examples of ancient Near Eastern wall painting from a site with Aramean heritage.

evidence.title: Hamath Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Hamath inscriptions comprise stone texts from Hama in both Luwian hieroglyphic and Aramaic traditions. Together they preserve royal names, titles, and historical references from a kingdom whose institutions and cultural affiliations changed over time; the corpus therefore documents interaction and succession rather than a simple bilingual system shared uniformly by all inhabitants.
evidence.significance: Shows the bilingual nature of the Hamath kingdom and Aramean cultural influence.
evidence.image_caption: Published facsimile of a Hamath inscription, representing the mixed Luwian and Aramaic inscriptional evidence from Hama.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; William Wright, The Empire of the Hittites (1886, public domain)

evidence.title: Hama Graffiti
evidence.description: The Hama graffiti are short, informal texts and names recorded in or around the excavated settlement of ancient Hamath. Unlike royal monuments, such marks can provide glimpses of ordinary writing practices and movement through urban spaces, but their fragmentary nature limits what can be inferred about the writers or the wider population.
evidence.significance: Evidence of everyday Aramaic use in the kingdom of Hamath.

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Bit-Hilani Palace
evidence.description: The Tell Halaf Bit-Hilani Palace consists of monumental architectural remains with carved basalt orthostats, caryatid figures, and a decorated gate area. The complex is associated with the Iron Age center of Guzana and demonstrates how architecture, sculpture, and controlled movement through the palace communicated authority, while the label bit-hilani remains a modern architectural classification rather than a complete description of the building's function.
evidence.significance: Best-preserved example of Aramean palatial architecture.
evidence.image_caption: Orthostats from the palace at Tell Halaf, shown as palace architecture rather than as a separate sculpture record.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons

evidence.title: Tell Halaf Inscription
evidence.description: The Tell Halaf Inscription, catalogued as KAI 231, was a limestone Aramaic monument from the Guzana context. The stele was photographed and published before being destroyed in Berlin during the Second World War, so surviving images and editions are now the primary means of studying a text whose original archaeological and architectural setting is only partly recoverable.
evidence.significance: Lost artifact documenting Aramean presence at Guzana.
evidence.image_caption: Historical photographs of the Gozan Pedestal/Tell Halaf inscription (KAI 231), recorded before the limestone stele was destroyed in Berlin in 1943.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Max von Oppenheim archive, Free University of Berlin (public domain)

evidence.title: Bukan Stele
evidence.description: The Bukan Stele is an Aramaic inscription from western Iran, associated with the late Achaemenid or early post-Achaemenid horizon. Its eastern findspot expands the geographic range of the Old Aramaic written record, while the surviving publication and the contextual image must be distinguished from claims about a single Aramean community or political authority at Bukan.
evidence.significance: Demonstrates the spread of Aramaic language and culture far beyond the Levant.
evidence.image_caption: Glazed brick from Qalaichi near Bukan, shown as contextual material from the site; it is not the Bukan Aramaic stele.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Negar Abdali

evidence.title: Neirab Stele I
evidence.description: Neirab Stele I is one of two funerary monuments from near Aleppo bearing an Aramaic text and an image of a priest associated with the local cult of the moon god.
evidence.significance: Important evidence for Aramean funerary practices and religious beliefs.

evidence.title: Tayma Stone
evidence.description: The Tayma Stone catalogued as KAI 228 is one of the separately numbered Aramaic stones from the Persian-period oasis of Tayma. The current image is representative of the Tayma inscription group.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in the Arabian Peninsula during the Achaemenid period.
evidence.image_caption: Representative photograph from the Tayma Stones group; object-specific photography is not yet recorded.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; User:Onceinawhile (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.title: Assur Ostracon and Tablets
evidence.description: The Assur Ostracon and Tablets comprise Aramaic letters and administrative texts recovered at the Assyrian capital. Their presence alongside Akkadian documents shows that Aramaic participated in written administration and communication, although the small and varied corpus cannot by itself measure how widely the language was spoken or used throughout the empire.
evidence.significance: Evidence that Aramaic was used alongside Akkadian in Assyrian administration.
evidence.image_caption: Assur ostracon (KAI 233), a 7th-century BCE Aramaic letter preserved in six fragments.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; scan from M. Lidzbarski, Altaramäische Urkunden aus Assur (1921, public domain)

evidence.title: Saqqara Aramaic Stele
evidence.description: The Saqqara Aramaic Stele is a funerary monument from Persian-period Egypt, dated here to 482 BC and preserved today through a published facsimile because the original is recorded as destroyed. Its Aramaic text documents an individual burial context and the presence of Aramaic writing in Egypt, not necessarily the migration or political rule of an Aramean population.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean presence in Egypt during the Achaemenid period.
evidence.image_caption: 1875 facsimile of the Saqqara Aramaic Stele (KAI 267; CIS II 122; TAD C20).
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Palaeographical Society (public domain)

evidence.title: Elephantine Papyri
evidence.museum: Various (Brooklyn Museum, Cairo Museum, Bodleian Library)
evidence.description: The Elephantine Papyri are a large group of Aramaic documents from a Persian-period island settlement in the Nile. Letters, contracts, petitions, and administrative records illuminate law, taxation, military service, family affairs, and religious institutions within a Jewish community, while also showing that Aramaic use took place inside the broader Achaemenid imperial system.
evidence.significance: Major source for Imperial Aramaic and daily life in the Persian Empire.

evidence.title: Hermopolis Aramaic Papyrus
evidence.description: TAD A2.4 is one of the eight Aramaic letters from the Hermopolis corpus in Persian-period Egypt. It is catalogued separately here by its TAD identifier; individual contents require the published edition.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic-speaking communities in Egypt and their social networks.
evidence.image_caption: Hermopolis Aramaic papyrus 4 (TAD A2.4), shown as representative evidence from the eight-letter Hermopolis corpus.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Ancient Egyptian papyri (public domain)

evidence.title: Sarıaydın Inscription
evidence.description: The Sarıaydın Inscription is a rock-cut Aramaic text from Cilicia in southern Anatolia, dated here to approximately 400 BC. Its location demonstrates that Aramaic writing reached Persian-period western Anatolia, but the inscription alone does not identify the writer's ethnicity or establish that the surrounding community was uniformly Aramaic-speaking.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic use in Anatolia during the Achaemenid period.

evidence.title: Daskyleion Stele I
evidence.museum: Museum of the Ancient Orient, Istanbul
evidence.description: Daskyleion Stele I is the marble funerary monument bearing the Aramaic text catalogued as KAI 318.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic as the administrative language of the Persian Empire in western Anatolia.
evidence.image_caption: Aramaic inscription on a Daskyleion stele (KAI 318), from the Istanbul Museum of the Ancient Orient.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Istanbul Museum of the Ancient Orient (public domain)

evidence.title: Luristan Aramaic Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Luristan Aramaic Inscriptions represent a group of texts reported from the highlands of western Iran and spanning more than one context or date. Their distribution is relevant to the history of Imperial and post-Imperial Aramaic writing, but the broad regional label and varied provenance require the individual inscriptions to be assessed separately.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic penetration into the Iranian highlands.
evidence.image_caption: Luristan bronze axe shown as regional context; it is not one of the Aramaic inscriptions in this corpus.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; SpeakingArch

evidence.title: Kandahar Bilingual Edict of Ashoka
evidence.description: The Kandahar Bilingual Rock Inscription combines Greek and Aramaic in an edict of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, dated to approximately 260 BC. It adapts imperial ethical and administrative communication for a region at the intersection of South Asian, Iranian, and Hellenistic worlds; it is therefore evidence for multilingual governance rather than an Aramean political monument.
evidence.significance: Demonstrates Aramaic as a language of international communication reaching Central Asia.
evidence.inscription_note: Aramaic script, transliteration, and English translation supplied for the inscription. Line divisions follow the sense of the supplied text and may differ from the original publication.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡔𐡍𐡍 𐡉 𐡐𐡕𐡉𐡕𐡅 𐡏𐡁𐡉𐡃 𐡆𐡉 𐡌𐡓𐡀𐡍 𐡐𐡓𐡉𐡃𐡀𐡓𐡔 𐡌𐡋𐡊𐡀 𐡒𐡔𐡉𐡈𐡀
inscription_lines.transliteration: šnn y ptytw ‘byd zy mr’n pryd’rš mlk’ qšyṭ’
inscription_lines.english_translation: Ten years having passed (?). It so happened (?) that our lord, King Priyadarśin, became the institutor of Truth.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡌𐡄𐡒𐡔𐡈𐡌𐡍 𐡀𐡃𐡉𐡍 𐡆𐡏𐡉𐡓 𐡌𐡓𐡏𐡀 𐡋𐡊𐡋𐡄𐡌 𐡀𐡍𐡔𐡍 𐡅𐡊𐡋𐡄𐡌 𐡀𐡃𐡅𐡔𐡉𐡀 𐡄𐡅𐡁𐡃𐡅𐡁𐡊𐡋 𐡀𐡓𐡒𐡀 𐡓𐡀𐡌 𐡔𐡕𐡉
inscription_lines.transliteration: mhqšṭmn ’dyn z‘yr mr‘’ lklhm ’nšn wklhm ’dwšy’ hwbdwbkl ’rq’ r’m šty
inscription_lines.english_translation: Since then, evil diminished among all men and all misfortunes were caused to disappear; and there was peace as well as joy throughout the whole earth.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡅𐡀𐡐 𐡆𐡉 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡊𐡌𐡀𐡊𐡋𐡀 𐡋𐡌𐡓𐡀𐡍 𐡌𐡋𐡊𐡀 𐡆𐡏𐡉𐡓𐡒𐡈𐡋𐡍
inscription_lines.transliteration: w’p zy znh km’kl’ lmr’n mlk’ z‘yrqṭln
inscription_lines.english_translation: Moreover, there was this concerning food: for our lord the king, only a few animals were killed.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡋𐡌𐡇𐡆𐡄 𐡊𐡋𐡄𐡌 𐡀𐡍𐡔𐡍 𐡀𐡕𐡄𐡇𐡎𐡉𐡍𐡍 𐡀𐡆𐡉 𐡍𐡅𐡍𐡉𐡀 𐡀𐡇𐡃𐡍𐡀𐡋𐡊
inscription_lines.english_translation: Having seen this, all men gave up the slaughter of animals; even those men who catch fish—the fishermen—were subject to prohibition.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡀𐡍𐡔𐡍 𐡐𐡕𐡉𐡆𐡁𐡕 𐡊𐡍𐡌 𐡆𐡉 𐡐𐡓𐡁𐡎𐡕 𐡄𐡅𐡉𐡍 𐡀𐡋𐡊
inscription_lines.english_translation: Similarly, those who were without restraint ceased to be without restraint.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡀𐡕𐡄𐡇𐡎𐡉𐡍𐡍 𐡌𐡍𐡐𐡓𐡁𐡎𐡕𐡉 𐡅𐡄𐡅𐡐𐡕𐡉𐡎𐡕𐡉 𐡋𐡀𐡌𐡅𐡄𐡉 𐡅𐡋𐡀𐡁𐡅𐡄𐡉 𐡅𐡋𐡌𐡆𐡉𐡔𐡕𐡉𐡀
inscription_lines.english_translation: And obedience to mother, father, and old men reigned in conformity with the obligations imposed by fate on each person.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡀𐡍𐡎𐡍𐡀𐡉𐡊 𐡀𐡎𐡓𐡄𐡉 𐡇𐡋𐡒𐡅𐡕𐡀 𐡅𐡋𐡀 𐡀𐡉𐡕𐡉 𐡃𐡉𐡍𐡀 𐡋𐡊𐡋𐡄𐡌 𐡀𐡍𐡔𐡉𐡀 𐡇𐡎𐡉𐡍𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡄𐡅𐡕𐡉𐡓
inscription_lines.transliteration: ’nsn’yk ’srhy ḥlqwt’ wl’ ’yty dyn’ lklhm ’nšy’ ḥsynznh hwtyr
inscription_lines.english_translation: And there was no Judgment for all the pious men.
This, the practice of Law, has been profitable to all men and will be more profitable in future.

evidence.image_caption: The Kandahar Sophytes Inscription, a related Hellenistic-period inscription from the Kandahar region; it is not the Ashoka bilingual rock inscription described here.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

evidence.title: Aramaic Inscription of Taxila
evidence.description: The Aramaic Inscription of Taxila is a text from the ancient city of Taxila in the northwestern Indian subcontinent, dated here to the third century BC. Its eastern location records the continued use of Aramaic beyond the former Achaemenid heartlands, while its wording and function must be interpreted from the surviving inscription and archaeological context rather than from geographic reach alone.
evidence.significance: Easternmost known Aramaic inscription, showing the language's reach to the Indian subcontinent.
evidence.inscription_note: The inscription is highly fragmentary. The 12 line divisions below follow the published table; translations are possible interpretations, and ellipses mark missing or uncertain text.

inscription_lines.english_translation: … memorial … (?)
… for creation(s) upon …; possibly a personal name related to Devadatta.
… the non-injury upon …
Possibly ‘true’ or ‘right’ … the non-injury …
… and to his father …
… good obedience; this …
… that …; possibly ‘good increase’.
Possibly ‘this’ or ‘good’ … ‘document’ … which is …
… our lord Priyadasi …
… going …
… and also his son(s) …
… of our lord Priyadasi …

evidence.image_caption: Aramaic inscription of Taxila (KAI 273), displayed at the Taxila Museum.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Onceinawhile (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.title: Pul-i-Darunteh Inscription
evidence.description: The Pul-i-Darunteh Inscription is an Aramaic rock text from the Jalalabad region, associated with the Mauryan emperor Ashoka and dated here to approximately 260 BC. The surviving reconstruction is presented as an eight-line sequence with original-script and transliteration fields; because the text is fragmentary and the English translations remain unfilled, its wording should not be treated as a complete translation or a secure statement of local identity.
evidence.significance: Further evidence of Aramaic use in the Mauryan Empire's western provinces.

inscription_lines.english_translation: [No?] living [being] is to be fattened [with other living beings?] …
… to be for people (that is, existing people) …
… to be seen—it is said—not [good] …
[… increase] of this object (that is, the practice of Dharma)—it is said—[caused] to increase …
… to see, to be seen—it is said …
… of the Beloved of the Gods [when] consecrated [for eight years]—it is said …
… in [outlying] towns—it is said … [all these instructions] were set (or put) to writing on pillars …
… [so that] they would be made known [to] whoever were (or would be) descendants …

evidence.image_caption: Transcription of the Lampaka (Pul-i-Darunteh) Aramaic inscription; this is a modern text reconstruction, not a photograph of the in-situ rock.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Pataliputra

evidence.title: A Long List of Supplies Disbursed
evidence.description: IA 17 is an individual Bactrian Aramaic manuscript document, a long list of supplies disbursed, dated 8 June 324 BC. It is one of 48 documents in the Khalili collection from ancient Bactria.
evidence.significance: Shows Aramaic functioning as the bureaucratic language of the Persian Empire in Central Asia.
evidence.image_caption: IA 17, A Long List of Supplies Disbursed, Bactria; the photograph is specific to this document.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Khalili Collections

evidence.title: Aramaic Inscription of Laghman
evidence.description: The Laghman Inscription is an Aramaic rock text from the Laghman valley attributed to Ashoka's Mauryan period. Its language and location show how an older imperial written tradition was used in a South Asian setting, while the inscription must be considered alongside the local landscape, the Mauryan political context, and the limits of the surviving reading.
evidence.significance: Part of the Ashokan edicts demonstrating Aramaic's role as a lingua franca in the East.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡁𐡔𐡍𐡕 𐡛 𐡗 𐡇𐡆𐡉 𐡗 𐡐𐡓𐡉𐡃𐡓𐡔 𐡌𐡋𐡊𐡀 𐡗 𐡓𐡒 𐡃𐡇𐡀
inscription_lines.transliteration: bšnt 10 ∣ ḥzy ∣ Prydrš mlkʾ ∣ rq dḥʾ
inscription_lines.english_translation: In the year 10, behold, the king Priyadasi expelled vanity from among prosperous men,
friends of that which is vain,

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡌𐡍 𐡔𐡓𐡉𐡓𐡉𐡍 𐡃𐡅𐡃𐡉 𐡌𐡄 𐡏𐡁𐡃 𐡓𐡉𐡒 𐡒𐡔𐡕𐡍
inscription_lines.transliteration: mn šryryn dwdy mh ʿbd ryq qštn
inscription_lines.english_translation: friends of those who fish fish-creatures.

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡙 𐡝 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡕𐡌𐡄 𐡕𐡃𐡌𐡓 𐡔𐡌𐡄 𐡆𐡍𐡄 𐡀𐡓𐡄𐡀 𐡊𐡍𐡐𐡕𐡉 𐡎𐡄𐡕𐡉
inscription_lines.transliteration: 200 znh rmh Tdmr šmh znh ʾrʾ knpty shty
inscription_lines.english_translation: At 200 ‘bows’, there is over there the place called Tadmor. This is the KNPTY road, that is to say (the road) of the Garden:

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡂𐡍𐡕𐡀 𐡉𐡕𐡓𐡉 𐡝 𐡜 𐡕𐡓𐡕𐡀 𐡕𐡍𐡄 𐡝 𐡏𐡋𐡀 𐡜 𐡜 𐡜 𐡜
inscription_lines.english_translation: More than 120 (‘bows’). At TRT’, here: 100. Above: 80.
Done with Wasu the judge

evidence.image_caption: Aramaic inscription of Laghman, an Aramaic rock inscription from the Laghman Valley in Afghanistan.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Pataliputra

evidence.title: Palmyrene Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Palmyrene Inscriptions are a large corpus of texts in the Palmyrene form of Aramaic, dating from the late Hellenistic and Roman periods. Funerary, dedicatory, civic, and commercial inscriptions record people, institutions, religious practices, and connections across the oasis city and its wider trading world; the corpus belongs to Palmyrene society rather than being a direct record of the Iron Age Aramean kingdoms.
evidence.significance: Largest corpus of Aramaic inscriptions from a single site. Documents Palmyrene society and Aramaic culture in the Roman period.
evidence.inscription_note: The lines below are a representative Palmyrene dedicatory inscription from the wider corpus. Line divisions follow the sense of the text rather than a publication layout; they should not be read as a complete transcription of every Palmyrene inscription or as a transcription of the pictured Louvre AO 2205 slab.

inscription_lines.english_translation: In commemoration of the One whose name is blessed.
Zabd'ateh, son of Hagagu, made it.
He was the son of Bar'ateh 'Alayb'al.
He made this incense altar for his life,

inscription_lines.original_script: 𐡅𐡋𐡇𐡉𐡉 𐡁𐡍𐡅𐡄𐡉 𐡅𐡀𐡇𐡅𐡄𐡉 𐡁𐡉𐡓𐡇 𐡍𐡉𐡎𐡍 𐡔𐡍𐡕 453
inscription_lines.transliteration: w-l-ḥyy bnhwy w-ʾḥwhy b-yrḥ Nysan šnt 453
inscription_lines.english_translation: and for the lives of his sons and brothers, in the month of Nisan, year 453.

evidence.image_caption: Representative Palmyrene funerary inscription on a limestone slab from Palmyra (Louvre AO 2205), dated 4 BC; one artifact within the wider Palmyrene inscription corpus.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Marie-Lan Nguyen (Jastrow) (public domain)

evidence.title: Aftuha Family Mosaic
evidence.description: The Aftuha Family Mosaic is a funerary floor mosaic from Edessa that depicts Aftuha and members of his family and includes a Syriac inscription. Its combination of image, text, and burial context provides evidence for family commemoration and the development of Syriac writing in the Roman-period city, without representing the whole of Edessan society.
evidence.significance: One of the earliest and best-preserved examples of Edessan Syriac art and epigraphy.

evidence.title: Orpheus Mosaic
evidence.description: The Orpheus Mosaic is a dated funerary mosaic from Edessa, made in AD 194, showing Orpheus and accompanied by a Syriac inscription. The text identifies the tomb owner and artist, linking an artistic scene with personal commemoration and providing a precisely dated example of Syriac epigraphic practice.
evidence.significance: Contains one of the earliest dated Syriac inscriptions known.

evidence.title: Funerary Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Edessa Funerary Inscriptions are a group of Syriac texts from tombs around ancient Urhay. Their epitaphs and commemorative formulas provide evidence for names, family relationships, burial practice, and language use across the second and third centuries AD, although the corpus represents selected funerary contexts rather than every social group in the city.
evidence.significance: Primary archaeological evidence for the language and culture of ancient Urhay.

evidence.title: Bethsaida Cultic Stele
evidence.description: The Bethsaida Cultic Stele is a broken basalt monument found near the monumental gate complex at et-Tell. Its horned bull-like head and dagger have been interpreted in relation to a storm or lunar deity, but the identification is not certain; the object is secure evidence for a cultic image and ritual setting, not by itself a complete description of the site's religion or political identity.
evidence.significance: Provides vivid physical evidence of Aramean religious iconography, cultic practices, and political influence within the kingdom of Geshur.

evidence.title: Hazael Ivory Bed (Nimrud)
evidence.description: The Hazael Ivory Bed fragment is an inscribed ivory object bearing the name Hazael of Aram-Damascus and listed here with the Nimrud corpus. The catalogue image and current identification require a provenance distinction: the documented Hazael-inscribed bed-related fragment is associated with Arslan Tash rather than Nimrud, so the object should not be used as secure evidence for a Nimrud findspot without qualification.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean luxury goods reaching Assyria, likely as tribute or war booty.
evidence.image_caption: Hazael-inscribed ivory bed fragment (KAI 232) from Arslan Tash. The Louvre identifies this fragment as the inscribed bed-related object; its documented findspot is Arslan Tash, not Nimrud.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Lamashtu2006 (CC BY-SA 4.0); Louvre object record

evidence.title: Sam’al Citadel Gate Lion
evidence.description: A monumental basalt guardian sculpture from the inner citadel gate at Zincirli. The inventory-specific record is retained separately from the other gate lions; the available image is representative of the group.
evidence.significance: Major examples of Aramean monumental sculpture combining local and Syro-Hittite traditions.
evidence.image_caption: Basalt lion sculptures from the inner citadel gate of Sam'al/Zincirli, displayed in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; User:Lusitana

evidence.title: Bar Rakib II
evidence.description: Bar-Rakib II (KAI 218) is the short inscription associated with the Berlin relief from Zincirli. It identifies Bar Rakkib, son of Panamu, and invokes Baal Harran; this object is kept separate from Bar-Rakib I (KAI 216), the twenty-line building inscription.
evidence.inscription_note: The two lines below follow the sense of the published English reading and use a normalized Aramaic-script reconstruction. They are not presented as a diplomatic facsimile; the exact KAI 218 edition and line layout should be checked against the primary publication.

inscription_lines.english_translation: My lord is Baal Harran.
I am Bar Rakkib, son of Panamu.

evidence.significance: Evidence for Bar-Rakib’s royal identity, religious language, and monumental self-representation.
evidence.image_caption: Relief associated with Bar-Rakib II (KAI 218), displayed in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; José Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro

evidence.title: Bethsaida City Gate
evidence.description: The Bethsaida City Gate is a large multi-chambered entrance complex in the Iron Age settlement at et-Tell, with associated high-place or cultic remains. Its walls, passageways, and adjacent installations provide evidence for settlement planning and public ritual, while the identification of et-Tell with Bethsaida and its association with Geshur remain historical reconstructions rather than uncontested facts.
evidence.significance: Best-preserved example of Aramean urban architecture in the southern Levant.
evidence.image_caption: City gate remains at et-Tell, the archaeological site identified by excavators with Bethsaida; that identification remains debated.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Bukvoed (CC BY 3.0)

evidence.title: Ein Gev Inscription
evidence.description: The Ein Gev Inscription is an Aramaic text from the lakeside settlement on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It has been used to discuss administrative or political activity connected with Aram-Damascus, but its limited context cannot by itself establish continuous control, the writer's identity, or a uniform population at Ein Gev.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramean administrative presence in the Galilee region.

evidence.title: Behistun Aramaic Inscription
evidence.description: The Behistun Aramaic Inscription is the Aramaic version of Darius I's monumental multilingual proclamation at Behistun. Carved into the rock face alongside the better-known Old Persian and Elamite versions, it demonstrates the role of Aramaic in imperial communication while requiring comparison with the other versions and with the monument's administrative setting.
evidence.significance: Key Imperial Aramaic text demonstrating the language's official status in the Achaemenid Empire.

evidence.title: Wadi Daliyeh Papyri
evidence.description: The Wadi Daliyeh Papyri are legal and administrative documents written in Aramaic and deposited in a cave in the Wadi Daliyeh region. Contracts concerning sales, loans, property, and personal status preserve the operation of law and administration in Persian-period Samaria, although the cave deposit reflects a particular group and historical moment rather than the whole province.
evidence.significance: Important source for Aramaic legal language and Persian-period administration in the Levant.
evidence.image_caption: Papyrus deed of slave sale from Wadi Daliyeh, shown after opening; representative evidence from the wider papyrus collection.
evidence.image_source: Israel Antiquities Authority, The Dead Sea Scrolls: Historical Timeline

evidence.title: Nabataean Inscriptions
evidence.description: The Nabataean Inscriptions form a large corpus of texts in the Nabataean variety of Aramaic from Petra, Sinai, and other parts of the Nabataean kingdom. Dedications, funerary texts, ownership marks, and public inscriptions record religious practice, personal names, trade, and political institutions across a long period of linguistic and cultural change; they should not be treated as a single uniform stage in the development of Arabic script.
evidence.significance: Major corpus documenting a late Aramaic dialect that evolved into early Arabic script.
evidence.image_caption: Nabataean inscriptions carved on a rock at Jabal al-Madbah, Petra.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons; Jean Housen (CC BY-SA 3.0)

evidence.title: Hatran Inscription
evidence.description: H 1 is an individually catalogued Hatran Aramaic inscription from Hatra. It belongs to the corpus of dedicatory, funerary, civic, and religious texts from the Parthian-period city; the individual text and object details require the relevant catalogue entry.
evidence.significance: Documents a distinct Eastern Aramaic dialect and the culture of a major Aramaic-speaking city in Parthian Mesopotamia.
evidence.image_caption: Representative photograph of a Hatran inscription from Hatra; this image is not specific to H 1.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons, Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.title: Dura-Europos Aramaic Texts
evidence.museum: Yale University Art Gallery / Damascus National Museum
evidence.description: The Dura-Europos Aramaic Texts include parchments, papyri, inscriptions, and shorter written records from the Roman-Parthian city on the Euphrates. Their varied formats and contexts show Aramaic operating alongside Greek, Latin, and Iranian languages in military, religious, domestic, and administrative settings, while the corpus reflects the diversity of a frontier city rather than one community's experience alone.
evidence.significance: Evidence of multilingual Aramaic use in a diverse frontier community.
evidence.image_caption: Inscription number 28 from the temple of Bel at Dura-Europos.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons, Franz Cumont (public domain)

evidence.title: Dead Sea Scrolls (Aramaic texts)
evidence.museum: Shrine of the Book, Israel Museum, Jerusalem
evidence.description: The Aramaic texts among the Dead Sea Scrolls include literary works such as the Genesis Apocryphon, Aramaic parts of 1 Enoch, the Targum of Job, and the Testament of Levi. Found in the Qumran corpus and dated across the late Second Temple period, they preserve narrative, interpretive, and religious traditions; their presence does not mean that all texts or all inhabitants of the region shared one language or identity.
evidence.significance: Major corpus of Jewish Aramaic literature preserving religious and literary traditions.
evidence.image_caption: The Genesis Apocryphon, an Aramaic literary work among the Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons, Geza Vermes (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.title: Samaria Papyri
evidence.description: The Samaria Papyri are administrative and legal documents written in Aramaic during the Persian period. Their records of sales, loans, and other transactions provide a close view of property, credit, and institutional practice in the province of Samaria, while the surviving group represents particular transactions rather than the complete legal life of the region.
evidence.significance: Evidence of Aramaic as the administrative language of the Persian province of Samaria.
evidence.image_caption: Papyrus deed of slave sale from Wadi Daliyeh, a representative Samaria papyrus found away from its place of composition.
evidence.image_source: Israel Antiquities Authority, The Dead Sea Scrolls: Historical Timeline

evidence.title: Sefire Stele II
evidence.museum: Damascus National Museum / National Museum of Beirut
evidence.description: Sefire Stele II is one of the three basalt treaty stelae from Sefire. The treaty records obligations, guarantees, sanctions, and divine witnesses in the early first millennium BC.
evidence.significance: Longest known Old Aramaic inscription. Key source for Aramaic treaty language and diplomacy.

evidence.title: Sefire Stele III
evidence.museum: Damascus National Museum / National Museum of Beirut
evidence.description: Sefire Stele III is one of the three basalt treaty stelae from Sefire. The treaty records obligations, guarantees, sanctions, and divine witnesses in the early first millennium BC.
evidence.significance: Longest known Old Aramaic inscription. Key source for Aramaic treaty language and diplomacy.

evidence.title: Neirab Stele II
evidence.description: Neirab Stele II is the second funerary monument from near Aleppo in the KAI 225–226 group, bearing an Aramaic text and priestly imagery associated with the local cult of the moon god.
evidence.significance: Important evidence for Aramean funerary practices and religious beliefs.

evidence.significance: Documents a distinct Eastern Aramaic dialect and the culture of a major Aramaic-speaking city in Parthian Mesopotamia.
evidence.image_caption: Representative photograph of a Hatran inscription from Hatra; this image is not specific to H 1121.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons, Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin (CC BY-SA 4.0)

evidence.title: Xi'an Stele (Jingjiao Stele)
evidence.description: The Xi'an Stele, traditionally called the Nestorian Stele, was erected in 781 during the Tang dynasty. Its main text is in Chinese and includes a Syriac inscription identifying the East Syriac Christian presence in China and describing the transmission of the Jingjiao, or Luminous Religion, from Daqin. The traditional label is retained as historical terminology, while Xi'an Stele and Jingjiao Stele are preferred descriptive names.
evidence.significance: Major evidence for East Syriac Christianity, Syriac literary culture, and Aramaic-speaking religious networks in Tang China.
evidence.image_caption: The Xi'an Stele (Jingjiao Stele) in the Beilin Museum, Xi'an, China.
evidence.image_source: Wikimedia Commons

evidence.title: Bar Rakib III
evidence.description: Bar Rakib III is a group of three small fragments from the Bar Rakib inscription corpus of Sam'al. The pieces were recorded in 1891; their individual text, original arrangement, and object context require the relevant published edition.
evidence.significance: Adds fragmentary evidence for the royal inscriptions and material culture of Sam'al under Bar Rakib.

evidence.title: Bar Rakib VIII
evidence.description: Bar Rakib VIII is an incomplete fragment preserving nine lines. The associated relief shows a bearded man holding a drinking vessel and a fan, with divine symbols above. The inscription expresses Bar Rakib's loyalty to Tiglath-Pileser, described as lord of the four quarters of the earth, and refers to the favor shown to him by the god Rakkab-El. The fragment was recorded in 1891; a verified line-by-line edition is not yet included.
evidence.significance: Combines royal inscriptional language and visual representation to document Bar Rakib's relationship with Assyria and Sam'al's religious-political world.
